record.original_question: Which parameters, or combinations of parameters, in a biological model can actually be inferred with useful precision from the available prior knowledge and observed data, especially in large models such as whole-cell models where many individual parameters may be practically non-identifiable?

evidence.quote: What we do find in many practical applications is that for any given dataset and model we can only infer some of the parameters (more generally some combinations of parameters); the rest are simply not inferable with any precision
Identifying which parameter combinations can be learned [20] from prior knowledge plus data will become a crucial part of parameterising large models, including whole cell models [21].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a parameterized biological model specified by a parameter vector θ ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ^p (for instance, an ODE, SDE, or stochastic reaction-network model of a cellular process, possibly a whole-cell model with very large p), an observation map y = h(θ) + noise mapping parameters to observable data, and a prior distribution π(θ) encoding existing biological knowledge. Given a finite dataset D drawn from such an observation process, develop a general methodology to determine:

(a) which individual components θ_i can be inferred from D together with π with useful precision (i.e., have posterior marginal variance substantially smaller than the prior variance, or admit a tight confidence region);

(b) which functional combinations φ(θ) (in particular, scalar combinations such as products, ratios, or sums φ(θ) = f(θ_{i_1}, …, θ_{i_k})) are practically identifiable from D and π even when the individual components θ_i are not; and

(c) for large-scale models where most individual parameters are practically non-identifiable, give a constructive algorithm that returns a maximal set of (approximately) identifiable parameter combinations together with quantitative precision guarantees, and characterize, as a function of the available prior knowledge and data, which combinations are learnable.

The problem is to provide a rigorous and computationally feasible framework that solves (a)–(c) for general nonlinear, high-dimensional biological models.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of identifying which parameters or parameter combinations are inferable in large biological models—particularly whole-cell models—remains an active area of research. Tools such as COMBOS and various structural/practical identifiability analyses exist for moderate-sized ODE systems, but symbolic methods become computationally prohibitive as model size grows, and no general solution is known for whole-cell-scale models. The DREAM8 challenge on whole-cell parameter identification highlighted that this remains an unsolved practical and theoretical problem.

status_evidence.title: On Finding and Using Identifiable Parameter Combinations in Nonlinear Dynamic Systems Biology Models (COMBOS)
status_evidence.snippet: Algorithms for identifying parameter combinations in ODE systems biology models; computational cost becomes prohibitive for large models.
status_evidence.claim: Partial methodology exists but does not scale to whole-cell models.

status_evidence.title: Parameter Identifiability Under Limited Experimental Data in Age-Structured Models of the Cell Cycle
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work on identifiability of cell-cycle models indicates ongoing research into which parameters can be learned from data.
status_evidence.claim: Identifiability of biological-model parameters remains an active research topic.

status_evidence.title: Identifiability analysis for stochastic differential equation models in systems biology
status_evidence.snippet: Identifiability analysis for SDE biological models is still under development.
status_evidence.claim: General identifiability frameworks for stochastic biological models are not yet complete.
